title: arxiv_2502.21242v1
universal_lens: Hierarchical graph models integrate domain features for long-term player re-identification under occlusion and motion variability. The hierarchical graph structure of SUSHI establishes a multi-scale topological isomorphism between discrete spatiotemporal detections and continuous kinematic flows. By embedding domain-specific categorical priors (jersey, team) into the edge-weighting kernel, we unify appearance-based re-identification with rigid geometric constraints, forming a robust manifold for tracking highly non-linear athlete trajectories.
gsi_mapping: Bayesian belief updates on tracklet continuity using team and jersey identifiers as probabilistic anchors in GSI's conformal predictive framework. GSI maps the binary edge classification in SUSHI to a conformal Bayesian inference problem. The MLP-encoded features act as likelihoods, while historical tracklet consistency provides the prior. We compute posterior probabilities for identity persistence across occlusions, utilizing conformal prediction sets to rigorously bound uncertainty in high-noise broadcast environments.
gse_mapping: Situationally grounded state transitions in GSE leverage graph-hierarchical tracklets to infer player identity and motion persistence across occlusions. In GSE, the transition from detection nodes to tracklet graphs represents state evolution under abrupt acceleration vectors. Situational reasoning utilizes the sports-domain features to resolve visual degeneracy among teammates. The linear program acts as a global constraint solver, ensuring physical plausibility of player transitions across the pitch.

primitives.name: Long-Term Player Tracking
primitives.verbatim_quote: Elder York University Toronto, Canada jelder@yorku.ca Abstract In team sports analytics, long-term player tracking remains a challenging task due to player appearance similarity, occlusion, and dynamic motion patterns.
primitives.assumptions: Players exhibit similar appearances; motion patterns vary dynamically; occlusions occur frequently.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When players are visually indistinguishable or temporarily obscured.

layer2.mapping: GSE's temporal state transition graph mirrors the tracking problem's graph hierarchy, where nodes represent player identities and edges encode motion continuity.
layer2.telemetry: Re-identification accuracy rate over extended absences.

primitives.name: Graph-Based Re-Identification
primitives.verbatim_quote: We introduce SportsSUSHI, a hierarchical graph-based approach that leverages domain-specific features, including jersey numbers, team IDs, and field coordinates, to enhance tracking accuracy.
primitives.assumptions: Domain-specific features provide discriminative cues; graph structure encodes spatial-temporal relationships.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When traditional appearance-based methods fail due to visual ambiguity.

layer2.mapping: GSI's kernel function computes similarity between tracklets using domain features, enabling robust association in high-occlusion environments.
layer2.telemetry: Precision of tracklet-to-tracklet matching based on feature overlap.

primitives.name: Domain-Specific Feature Integration
primitives.verbatim_quote: The inclusion of domain-specific features in our approach significantly improves association accuracy, as demonstrated in our experiments.
primitives.assumptions: Jersey numbers, team IDs, and field positions are reliable identifiers.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Under conditions of low visual distinctiveness or partial occlusion.

layer2.mapping: GSE's feature space aligns with domain-specific cues, allowing for consistent identification across frames.

primitives.name: Hierarchical Tracking Framework
primitives.verbatim_quote: Player tracking is a specific case of a well-studied topic in computer vision - Multi-Object Tracking (MOT).
primitives.assumptions: Short-term tracking provides initial associations; long-term coherence requires hierarchical refinement.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When short-term tracking fails to maintain persistent identities through occlusions.

layer2.mapping: GSI's hierarchical inference engine applies MOT principles to construct stable player trajectories via multi-scale temporal alignment.

primitives.name: Hierarchical Graph Association Operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: Due to its ability to capture long-term associations, SUSHI is well-suited for the task of long-term tracking.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: G: Directed acyclic graph (dimensionless), V: Set of detection nodes (count), E: Set of temporal edges (count), L: Hierarchical level index (integer)
primitives.assumptions: Assumes Markovian property holds within local temporal windows; assumes feature extraction yields stationary distributions across varying camera angles.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks down when occlusion duration exceeds the maximum temporal span of the highest hierarchical graph level, or during complete loss of visual signal.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic mapping of SUSHI's multi-level graph construction to GSE's temporal state-transition manifolds, where higher levels represent macroscopic tactical shifts rather than microscopic kinematics.

primitives.name: Domain-Specific Feature Embedding Kernel
primitives.verbatim_quote: Player tracking leverages both appearance and kinematic features, as in MOT, but requires additional sports-specific features like team IDs and jersey numbers due to the visual similarity among teammates [42, 49, 53].
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: f_app: Appearance feature vector (dimensionless embedding), f_kin: Kinematic feature vector (m/s, m/s^2), f_dom: Domain categorical feature (team ID, jersey number) (dimensionless integer)
primitives.assumptions: Assumes OCR and team-color segmentation modules operate with bounded error rates; assumes distinct jersey numbers are visible at least intermittently.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails under severe motion blur rendering jersey numbers unreadable, or during night games with poor illumination causing color space collapse.

layer2.mapping: Derives a composite affinity matrix for GSI by concatenating standard re-ID embeddings with one-hot encoded domain priors, drastically reducing the collision space in high-density clusters.
layer2.telemetry: Identity Switch (IDS) rate reduction compared to baseline appearance-only trackers.

primitives.name: Non-Linear Kinematic Solver
primitives.verbatim_quote: Unlike pedestrians, players exhibit abrupt, non-linear movements, which tracking methods often address [24,26,40,51].
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: a(t): Instantaneous acceleration vector (m/s^2), v(t): Velocity vector (m/s), \Delta t: Discrete time step (s)
primitives.assumptions: Assumes player dynamics can be approximated by piecewise polynomial splines rather than constant velocity models; assumes frame-rate is sufficient to capture peak accelerations.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularities occur if sampling frequency is too low to satisfy the Nyquist-Shannon theorem for rapid directional changes, leading to aliasing in trajectory reconstruction.

layer2.mapping: Maps directly to GSE's situational reasoning engine, replacing standard Kalman filters with adaptive, non-linear state predictors that account for sport-specific burst mechanics.
layer2.telemetry: Trajectory smoothness metrics and deviation from ground-truth paths during high-acceleration events.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSI conformal predictive regions via graph convolutional posterior calibration and to GSE state-transition matrices through edge flow propagation.

The approach integrates domain-specific features—jersey numbers, team IDs, and field coordinates—into a graph structure that supports both short-term and long-term tracking. This formulation enables robust re-identification even when players are visually ambiguous or temporarily hidden. The model's design reflects a synthesis of computer vision and structured reasoning, where graph hierarchies act as a semantic scaffold for temporal continuity. From a foundational perspective, this work bridges the gap between generic MOT frameworks and sport-specific demands, offering a principled approach to player tracking that accounts for both appearance and contextual cues. reasoning_traces.think: The foundational shift presented in this chapter window is the transition from generic Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) paradigms—predominantly designed for linear pedestrian or vehicular dynamics—to a specialized Multiple Athlete Tracking (MAT) framework. Standard MOT relies heavily on constant velocity assumptions and purely appearance-based Re-ID, which fundamentally fails in the high-frequency, non-linear kinematic regime of professional sports. The introduction of the SUSHI (SportsSUSHI) architecture addresses this by constructing a hierarchical graph representation. At the base level, nodes represent raw detections, connected by edges weighted through a combination of spatial proximity and deep appearance embeddings. However, the critical epistemic leap occurs through the integration of domain-specific categorical priors: jersey numbers and team IDs. These features act as hard constraints within the soft probabilistic framework of the graph neural network (GNN). By employing weight-sharing mechanisms across hierarchical levels, the system learns to dynamically adjust the importance of these features based on temporal distance. Short-term tracklets rely more heavily on kinematic continuity and fine-grained appearance, whereas long-term associations leverage the invariant nature of jersey numbers and team colors. This hierarchical approach effectively decouples the immediate, noisy dynamics of player movement from the persistent, structural identity of the athletes. The mathematical formulation translates this into a series of binary edge classification tasks solved via neural message passing, ultimately converted into final trajectories through a linear programming relaxation. This ensures global optimality in track assignment while respecting local feature affinities, providing a robust solution to the severe occlusion and visual similarity challenges inherent in broadcast sports video.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage of this primitive traces back to classical Kalman filtering and Hungarian algorithm-based assignment in early MOT. It evolved through Deep SORT's incorporation of CNN-based appearance features. The specific push toward MAT was historically stalled by a lack of large-scale annotated datasets. The retrocausal catalyst here is the release of SoccerNet and SportsMOT, which provided the necessary empirical grounding to shift focus from generic object tracking to domain-aware, hierarchical graph-based association, explicitly accounting for sports semantics.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Modeling the opposing agents in this context involves understanding the cognitive load of both the players and the tracking algorithm. Players execute abrupt, non-linear maneuvers designed to deceive opponents and evade markers. A naive tracker interprets these as noise or identity switches. SportsSUSHI embodies a 'theory of mind' by anticipating these deceptive kinematic bursts. It understands that a sudden change in velocity vector does not necessarily imply a new identity, especially if supported by consistent jersey number recognition. Furthermore, it accounts for the collective behavior of teams, using team IDs to constrain the search space, recognizing that players from the same team rarely occupy the exact same spatial coordinates simultaneously without occlusion.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Anti-collinearity and leakage vetoes are crucial to prevent the model from over-relying on a single feature modality. For instance, if two players wear similar colored jerseys and run in parallel, appearance and team ID features become collinear and uninformative. The cross-layer veto mechanism must detect this degeneracy and temporarily elevate the weight of kinematic divergence or pose extraction features. Conversely, during severe motion blur, visual features may leak noise into the kinematic solver; the system must veto unreliable OCR outputs and fall back to pure trajectory extrapolation. Ensuring these vetoes function correctly prevents catastrophic identity swaps during critical, high-speed play sequences.
